title: Introduction to Redis
subtitle: What Redis is, its use cases, and architecture
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Databases like PostgreSQL are great for structured queries but require disk I/O. For use cases like session storage, counters, and caching, hitting the database on every request creates latency and load.
whyItExists.solution: Redis stores data in RAM, delivering sub-millisecond reads and writes. It supports rich data structures beyond simple key-value, so it handles queues, leaderboards, pub/sub, and rate limiting natively.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Caching, session management, real-time leaderboards, rate limiting, job queues, pub/sub notifications, and any workload requiring very high throughput.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Primary data store for large datasets that must outlive memory, complex relational queries, or when you need ACID transactions across many entities.

explainModes.beginner: Redis is like a super-fast sticky note board. Instead of writing to a heavy notebook (your database), you stick notes on a whiteboard (RAM) for quick answers.
explainModes.simple: Redis is an in-memory key-value store. Think of it as a dictionary that lives in RAM — blazing fast, but needs to be backed up to survive restarts.
explainModes.standard: Redis is an in-memory data structure server. It stores data as key-value pairs in RAM, delivering microsecond latency. It supports strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, and streams as native types.
explainModes.technical: Redis is a single-threaded, event-loop-based in-memory data store. Data lives in RAM, with optional persistence via RDB snapshots or AOF logging. It exposes a command-based protocol (RESP) over TCP, achieves >1M ops/sec on commodity hardware, and supports atomic operations, Lua scripting, and cluster mode for horizontal scale.
explainModes.deepDive: Redis uses a reactor pattern with an epoll/kqueue event loop. The single-thread model eliminates lock contention. Memory is managed via jemalloc. Persistence uses a background fork() for RDB and a write-ahead log for AOF. Cluster mode uses consistent hashing over 16384 slots with gossip-based failure detection. Redis 7+ added multi-part AOF to reduce atomic rename overhead at AOF rewrite time.

content.text: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an open-source, in-memory data structure store. Because it stores data in RAM rather than on disk, it delivers sub-millisecond response times and can handle millions of operations per second on a single node.

content.definition: Data is stored in RAM rather than on disk. Access is nanoseconds instead of milliseconds, but data may be lost on restart unless persistence is configured.
Every piece of data is stored and retrieved by a unique string key. The value can be a string, list, set, hash, sorted set, stream, and more.

content.code:
# macOS
brew install redis
brew services start redis

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt update && sudo apt install redis-server -y
sudo systemctl start redis

# Docker (easiest for local dev)
docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine

# Connect with redis-cli
redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> PING
PONG
127.0.0.1:6379> SET hello world
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET hello
"world"

content.text: Redis achieves its speed from three design decisions: data lives in RAM (no disk I/O), Redis is single-threaded (no lock contention), and it uses a non-blocking I/O event loop (thousands of concurrent connections without threads).

content.title: Redis vs a SQL Database for Caching

a.name: Redis
weaknesses: No complex joins or transactions across keys
a.useWhen: Caching, sessions, counters, queues, real-time features

b.name: PostgreSQL
b.useWhen: Primary data store, complex queries, financial data

items: Caching — Store database query results or API responses with a TTL to reduce load
Session storage — Keep user sessions in Redis instead of a database for fast auth
Rate limiting — Use atomic counters to limit requests per user per second
Leaderboards — Sorted sets maintain ranked lists automatically
Job queues — Lists support blocking push/pop for background workers
Pub/Sub — Broadcast events to multiple subscribers in real time
Distributed locks — SET NX EX implements a lightweight mutex

content.text: Redis is single-threaded for command execution. This eliminates race conditions on data structures without needing locks — a INCR is always atomic.
Redis stores everything in RAM. Without persistence configured, a restart means data loss. Enable RDB snapshots or AOF before going to production.
Redis keys are just strings, but a good naming convention prevents collisions and makes debugging easy. Use colon-separated namespaces: object:id:field.

content.code:
# Good key naming patterns
user:1001:profile       # user object
user:1001:sessions      # list of session IDs
session:abc123          # session data
rate:api:192.168.1.1    # rate limit counter
cache:product:42        # cached product
leaderboard:weekly      # sorted set

# Avoid:
user1001profile         # no separator
USER:1001               # inconsistent case

questions.question: Where does Redis primarily store data?
questions.explanation: Redis stores all data in RAM for maximum speed. This is why it can serve millions of operations per second.

questions.question: Why is Redis single-threaded?
options: To eliminate lock contention and race conditions on data structures
questions.explanation: Single-threading means commands execute atomically without needing locks, simplifying the data model and eliminating deadlocks.

questions.question: Which use case is Redis NOT typically the best choice for?
options: Primary store for a 10TB financial database
questions.explanation: Redis data must fit in RAM. A 10TB financial database would require enormous (and expensive) RAM. Use PostgreSQL or a disk-based database for primary data storage at that scale.

faq.a: Yes. Redis supports RDB (periodic snapshots to disk) and AOF (append-only log of every write). The recommended setup is hybrid: AOF with RDB preamble.

faq.q: How much data can Redis hold?
faq.a: Limited only by available RAM. A single Redis instance can hold tens of GBs. Use Redis Cluster for datasets that exceed a single machine's memory.
Redis was open source under BSD until 2024. Redis 7.4+ uses a dual license (RSALv2 / SSPLv1). Valkey is the community fork that remains BSD-licensed.
